screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we explore advanced concurrency strategies you’ll use to keep PostgreSQL systems fast and correct under load. We’ll compare pessimistic locking, where you acquire exclusive locks before modifying rows, with optimistic locking, where you detect conflicts at write time using a version or timestamp. You will see how PostgreSQL’s SELECT FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED and NOWAIT clauses let worker pools pick tasks without blocking, and we’ll study the invisible but critical danger of transaction ID wraparound and how VACUUM and autovacuum prevent it. Concrete examples include an accounts update using FOR UPDATE, an optimistic update that checks a version column, and a tasks queue demo showing two workers selecting different rows. I’ll also point out common mistakes — long-running transactions, excessive table-level locking, and unnecessary FOR UPDATE — and show which monitoring views to consult when things slow down. By the end you will know the trade-offs of each pattern, how to implement queue workers safely, and what to monitor so your database continues to operate reliably. How might you apply these patterns to the systems you manage, and which pitfall could cause the most trouble in your environment?

Design for throughput and correctness. Compare optimistic and pessimistic approaches, learn queue-processing patterns with SKIP LOCKED and NOWAIT, and understand XID wraparound and VACUUM.

Locking strategies, queue workers, XID wraparound, and monitoring tips.

screens.title: Pessimistic Locking (SELECT FOR UPDATE)
screens.narratorSegment: Pessimistic locking is a pattern that assumes conflicts are likely and therefore holds locks before modifications occur. In PostgreSQL the canonical form is SELECT... FOR UPDATE, which acquires an exclusive lock on selected rows so other transactions cannot modify them until you commit or roll back. An everyday example is transferring funds between bank accounts: you might SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE account_id = 123 FOR UPDATE; then verify and write the new balance inside the same transaction. The benefit is correctness — you avoid lost updates — but the downside is blocking: other transactions that need the same rows will wait. A common misconception is that FOR UPDATE is always safer. In low-contention workloads it simply adds overhead and can cause unnecessary blocking because MVCC already isolates readers from writers. Use FOR UPDATE when you need strict serialization of a critical section, and keep transactions short to avoid holding locks for long periods. Key takeaway: pessimistic locking buys safety at the cost of throughput, so apply it only when conflict likelihood justifies the blocking behavior. How might you limit the window a lock is held in your application logic?

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.6 › Pessimistic Locking
Definition

Pessimistic locking acquires exclusive locks on rows before updates to prevent concurrent writes from intervening.

When to use
  • Critical sections where stale writes would cause incorrect state.
  • High-value updates where blocking is acceptable for correctness.
Key Takeaway

FOR UPDATE is safe for serialization. Minimize transaction length to reduce blocking.

Example
BEGIN;
SELECT balance FROM accounts
WHERE account_id = 123
FOR UPDATE;
-- check balance and perform transfer
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100 WHERE account_id = 123;
COMMIT;
Common mistake
Using FOR UPDATE for reads where MVCC would suffice adds blocking with no benefit. Avoid unnecessary locks on read-only flows.
Pro tip
If you must lock, do it in a short transaction and acquire locks in a consistent order to reduce deadlocks.

screens.title: Optimistic Locking with Version Columns
screens.narratorSegment: Optimistic locking assumes conflicts are rare and allows concurrent read and modify operations, detecting collisions only when a transaction writes. The typical implementation is to add a version column — an integer or a last_updated timestamp — to each row. When reading, the application records the current version. At update time it includes that original version in the WHERE clause and increments it. If another transaction updated the row in the meantime, the WHERE clause will match zero rows, signaling a conflict. For example, update products set stock = 9, version = 2 where product_id = 1 and version = 1; either the update affects one row and you succeed, or it affects zero rows and your application must retry or surface a conflict to the user. A common misconception is that optimistic locking eliminates the need to think about conflicts; it does not. You must design retry policies and user feedback paths, especially where updates are frequent. Optimistic locking maximizes concurrency in low-conflict workloads and shifts complexity into application logic for conflict handling. Optimistic Locking with Version Columns means detect conflicts at write-time using version checks; retry or resolve on zero-row updates.. In practical terms, detect conflicts at write time using versions or timestamps. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.6 › Optimistic Locking
Definition

Optimistic locking allows concurrent changes and detects conflicts at commit using a version or timestamp check.

Why it helps
  • Maximizes concurrency for low-conflict workloads.
  • Shifts conflict resolution into application logic for flexibility.
Key Takeaway

Use optimistic locking when conflicts are rare and you can handle retries or merges in the application.

Example SQL
-- Read
SELECT description, version FROM products WHERE product_id = 123;
-- Suppose version = 5

-- Update attempt with optimistic lock
UPDATE products
SET description = 'New description', version = 6
WHERE product_id = 123 AND version = 5;
-- If 1 row updated -> success; if 0 rows -> conflict, retry or resolve
Misconception
Optimistic locking won’t automatically merge changes. Your application must decide how to retry or prompt the user to reconcile updates.
Analogy
Think of optimistic locking as two people editing a shared note; both can type, but when one saves, the app checks whether the base version changed and asks for reconciliation if needed.

screens.title: Queue Processing with SKIP LOCKED
screens.narratorSegment: When multiple workers consume tasks from a shared table, you want each worker to acquire a unique row without getting blocked by locks held by others. SELECT... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED is designed for exactly that. The pattern: start a transaction, select one pending job ordered by created_at using FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED LIMIT 1, then update the row to mark it processing and commit. SKIP LOCKED tells PostgreSQL to ignore rows that are already locked by another transaction instead of waiting. The practical result is that workers graze the queue and immediately claim available tasks, improving throughput and avoiding idle waiting. A concrete flow: Worker A begins and locks job 1; Worker B issues the same SELECT with SKIP LOCKED and PostgreSQL skips job 1 and returns job 2. Worker B can proceed without waiting for Worker A to commit. A common misconception is that SKIP LOCKED silently loses tasks; it does not lose rows, it only skips rows currently locked, so unprocessed tasks remain available. Use SKIP LOCKED for competing consumers when you prefer fast claim-over-wait semantics. The key question to reflect on: how will your application detect and re-enqueue jobs that fail after being claimed?

keyIdea.text: Use SKIP LOCKED for non-blocking worker pools so each worker claims an unlocked row immediately.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.6 › SKIP LOCKED
Process Steps
1. Begin transaction
Open a short transaction to limit lock time.
2. Select FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
Atomically lock an available row or skip any locked rows.
3. Update and commit
Mark job as processing and commit to release locks.
Example SQL Sequence
BEGIN;
SELECT * FROM job_queue
WHERE status = 'pending'
ORDER BY created_at
FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
LIMIT 1;
-- process the returned row, then
UPDATE job_queue SET status = 'processing' WHERE job_id = ;
COMMIT;
Concrete example
Two workers run the same SELECT; the first locks one row, the second skips it and selects the next pending row, so both proceed concurrently.
Edge case
If a worker crashes after claiming a job, you must detect and retry or requeue the job since SKIP LOCKED will not reassign locked-but-uncommitted rows until the lock is released.
Key Takeaway

SKIP LOCKED is ideal for high-throughput worker pools that prefer to skip locked rows rather than wait.

screens.title: NOWAIT vs SKIP LOCKED
screens.narratorSegment: SELECT... FOR UPDATE NOWAIT and FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED are two related behaviors that differ in how they treat locked rows. NOWAIT immediately raises an error if a requested lock cannot be acquired; this is useful when you prefer to fail fast and handle the error rather than silently skip rows. SKIP LOCKED, by contrast, ignores locked rows and returns the next unlocked row, which is ideal for horizontally scaled worker pools. A concrete scenario clarifies the contrast: suppose a single consumer expects to process the next item in strict order; using NOWAIT ensures that if another process is handling that first item, your code gets an immediate error and can decide to retry or abort. In a multi-worker setup where order is unimportant, SKIP LOCKED lets workers continue processing other jobs without blocking. A common misconception is that NOWAIT is always unsafe; it’s not — it’s appropriate when ordering or strict ownership semantics matter and you want immediate feedback. Choose NOWAIT when you need explicit failure behavior and SKIP LOCKED when you favor availability and throughput. NOWAIT vs SKIP LOCKED means nowait fails fast on locked rows; skip locked skips locked rows and returns the next available one.. In practical terms, fail fast or skip locked rows — choose based on your failure semantics. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.6 › NOWAIT vs SKIP LOCKED
FOR UPDATE NOWAIT

If the selected row is locked, NOWAIT immediately raises an error instead of blocking or skipping.

  • Use when ordering matters or you want explicit failure handling.
  • Prevents silent skipping; requires error handling and retries.
FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED

Skip locked rows and return the next unlocked row, avoiding waits and increasing throughput for many consumers.

  • Best for horizontally scaled worker pools.
  • Requires handling of worker crashes and requeueing policies.
Concrete scenario
Single-worker ordering -> NOWAIT to detect locks; many-workers where order is flexible -> SKIP LOCKED to avoid blocking.
Common mistake
Using SKIP LOCKED when strict ordering is required can lead to unintended out-of-order processing.

screens.title: Hands-on: SKIP LOCKED with Two Workers
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a concrete hands-on demonstration using the provided tasks table. Create the tasks table, insert a few pending tasks, then simulate two psql sessions. Worker 1 opens a transaction and runs SELECT... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED LIMIT 1; it locks one row but does not commit immediately. content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.6 › Live Coding: SKIP LOCKED
Starter Schema
CREATE TABLE tasks (
  task_id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  description TEXT NOT NULL,
  status VARCHAR(50) DEFAULT 'pending',
  assigned_worker_id INT,
  created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT NOW(),
  processed_at TIMESTAMP
);

INSERT INTO tasks (description) VALUES
('Process image A'),
('Generate report B'),
('Send email C');
Simulated sessions
-- Worker 1 (Session 1)
BEGIN;
SELECT task_id, description FROM tasks
WHERE status = 'pending'
ORDER BY created_at
FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
LIMIT 1;
-- Worker 1 locks task 1, DO NOT COMMIT YET

-- Worker 2 (Session 2)
BEGIN;
SELECT task_id, description FROM tasks
WHERE status = 'pending'
ORDER BY created_at
FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
LIMIT 1;
-- Worker 2 receives next unlocked task
UPDATE tasks SET status = 'processing', assigned_worker_id = 2, processed_at = NOW()
WHERE task_id = ;
COMMIT;

-- Worker 1 finishes
UPDATE tasks SET status = 'processing', assigned_worker_id = 1, processed_at = NOW()
WHERE task_id = ;
COMMIT;
Observation
Worker 2 does not block on Worker 1's locked row; each worker processes a different task.
Remember
Ensure you have logic to detect crashed workers and requeue tasks if a worker dies while holding a lock.
Key Takeaway

SKIP LOCKED allows concurrent workers to claim tasks without blocking, improving throughput in worker pools.

screens.title: Transaction ID (XID) Wraparound
screens.narratorSegment: PostgreSQL assigns a 32-bit transaction ID (XID) to each transaction. Because it’s a fixed-size counter, after roughly two billion transactions the counter will wrap around. When wraparound occurs, PostgreSQL can no longer reliably decide whether an old row version is visible to a given transaction unless old XIDs are frozen. VACUUM — and the autovacuum daemon — periodically scan tables and mark very old XIDs as frozen, making those rows permanently visible for visibility checks. If autovacuum is not configured or long-running transactions prevent VACUUM from freezing rows, the database risks corruption or forced shutdown to avoid data integrity issues. Monitor pg_stat_database. datname and age(datfrozenxid) to see xid_age for your database. The common misconception is that VACUUM is optional; in practice autovacuum is essential to prevent wraparound. As a practical rule, ensure autovacuum runs regularly and investigate databases with high xid_age before they approach dangerous thresholds. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 5 › Chapter 4.6 › XID Wraparound
What is XID wraparound?

PostgreSQL uses 32-bit transaction IDs. After about two billion transactions the counter wraps and old XIDs must be frozen or visibility checks fail.

Role of VACUUM

VACUUM marks old transaction IDs as frozen so PostgreSQL can determine visibility even after wraparound. autovacuum automates this process.

Key Takeaway

Keep autovacuum healthy; monitor xid_age and avoid long-running transactions that block VACUUM.

Monitoring Query
SELECT datname,
  age(datfrozenxid) AS xid_age,
  datfrozenxid
FROM pg_database
WHERE datname = current_database();
Pitfall
Long-lived transactions prevent VACUUM from freezing tuples and can cause xid_age to grow dangerously large.
Concrete check
If xid_age climbs, investigate autovacuum settings and active long-running transactions via pg_stat_activity to resolve blockers.

screens.title: Long-Running Transactions & Excessive Locking
screens.narratorSegment: Long-running transactions are one of the most damaging concurrency pitfalls. When a transaction remains open for hours or days it holds onto snapshot state and locks, preventing VACUUM from marking tuples as removable or freezing old XIDs. This leads to table bloat as dead row versions accumulate, and it can increase xid_age, bringing the database closer to wraparound risk. Excessive locking — especially coarse table-level locks — reduces parallelism and increases blocking and deadlocks. A common example is acquiring locks in inconsistent order across transactions; this pattern easily produces deadlocks under concurrent access. Another frequent mistake is blanket use of FOR UPDATE on many rows when only a simple SELECT would suffice; this adds unnecessary lock contention. To mitigate these issues, keep transactions short, avoid manual long transactions in application code, use row-level locking when possible, and acquire locks in a consistent order. Regularly examine pg_stat_activity for idle-in-transaction sessions and pg_locks for blocking chains so you can quickly identify and resolve these problems. Module 5 › Chapter 4.6 › Long Transactions & Locks
Why long transactions are bad
  • They prevent VACUUM from removing old row versions and freezing XIDs.
  • They hold locks that block other transactions and reduce concurrency.
  • They contribute to table bloat and increased xid_age.
Mitigations
  • Keep transactions short and do non-DB work outside transactions.
  • Avoid table-level locks; prefer row-level locking and consistent lock ordering.
Check for offenders
Inspect pg_stat_activity for long-running or idle-in-transaction sessions and act to close or fix them.
Deadlock risk
Inconsistent lock acquisition order between transactions is a leading cause of deadlocks; standardize lock order to avoid them.
Key Takeaway

Short transactions and consistent lock ordering reduce blocking, bloat, and wraparound exposure.

screens.title: Inspecting Locks and Activity
screens.narratorSegment: When concurrency issues appear you must be able to inspect what the server is doing. pg_stat_activity shows active sessions, their state, and query text so you can spot long-running or idle-in-transaction sessions. pg_locks reveals which locks are held and which processes are waiting; it helps you trace blocking chains. pg_stat_statements identifies heavy or frequently contended queries for optimization. A concrete troubleshooting workflow: query pg_stat_activity to find sessions with long durations, join to pg_locks to see which sessions are waiting for locks and which sessions hold those locks, and use pg_stat_statements to find the offending query text and plan characteristics. A common misconception is that killing a waiting session always fixes the problem; sometimes the blocker is the session holding a lock, not the waiter. Prefer addressing the blocker or fixing the root cause in application logic. Key practical steps include collecting the session IDs, identifying lock types and targets, and then applying targeted remedies such as terminating a runaway session or rewriting a hot query to reduce lock contention. Module 5 › Chapter 4.6 › Monitoring
Useful views
  • pg_stat_activity — active sessions and their queries.
  • pg_locks — active locks and waiting relationships.
  • pg_stat_statements — slow or frequent queries that create contention.
Troubleshooting steps
  1. Use pg_stat_activity to find long-running transactions.
  2. Inspect pg_locks to find blockers and waiters.
  3. Check pg_stat_statements to optimize offending queries.
Example check
-- Find long transactions
SELECT pid, now() - query_start AS runtime, state, query
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE state <> 'idle'
ORDER BY runtime DESC
LIMIT 10;
Misconception
Killing the waiter is usually ineffective; identify and act on the session that holds the lock instead.
Key Takeaway

Use a combined view of sessions, locks, and statements to locate root causes and apply focused remediation.

screens.title: Design Patterns & Common Remedies
screens.narratorSegment: This screen collects practical design rules that reduce concurrency problems. First, always acquire locks in a consistent global order to avoid deadlocks — pick a deterministic ordering of resources and stick to it across transactions. Second, keep transactions short: do not perform long-running external calls while holding database locks or doing important updates. Third, prefer row-level locks instead of table-level locks when you need to serialize updates. Fourth, instrument and monitor: alert on idle-in-transaction sessions and rising xid_age. Fifth, for worker queues use SKIP LOCKED and implement a robust failure/retry policy so claimed tasks are retried if a worker crashes. A frequent misconception is that more aggressive locking configurations will always increase safety; in fact, coarse locks often reduce throughput and lead to cascading waits. The end takeaway is to make small, incremental changes: tune autovacuum, standardize lock order, shorten transactions, and add visibility through monitoring queries. Lock ordering
Pick a stable order for acquiring multiple locks to avoid circular waits and deadlocks.
Short transactions
Perform non-database work outside transactions and commit quickly to free locks and allow VACUUM to progress.
Row-level locks
Prefer row locks over table-level locks for finer concurrency control.
SKIP LOCKED + retry
Use SKIP LOCKED for workers and implement requeue policies for tasks claimed but not completed due to crashes.
Autovacuum tuning
Ensure autovacuum runs frequently enough for busy tables so XIDs are frozen before wraparound risk.
Monitoring
Alert on high xid_age, blocked queries, and many idle-in-transaction sessions to catch problems early.
Key Takeaway

Small, consistent discipline in lock ordering, transaction length, and monitoring prevents most concurrency failures.

screens.title: Lab: Implement and Test Optimistic Locking
screens.narratorSegment: This lab asks you to implement optimistic locking for a products table using a version column and to exercise a conflict. Steps: add version INT to products, read the current description and version in one session, then in a second session update the same row and commit. In the first session attempt an UPDATE that includes the original version in the WHERE clause and increments the version. If the UPDATE affects zero rows you have detected a conflict and should retry or present the user with the latest data. The purpose is to observe the optimistic pattern: concurrent reads proceed, and only conflicting writes force application-level conflict resolution. A common mistake is to forget to check the rows-affected count after the UPDATE; without that check the application will assume success and silently lose changes. After completing the exercise, discuss what retry policy you would implement: immediate retry, exponential backoff, or user-driven merge. Which policy fits your product's expectations around freshness and user experience? Module 5 › Chapter 4.6 › Optimistic Locking Lab
Starter steps
-- Add a version column
ALTER TABLE products ADD COLUMN version INT DEFAULT 1;

-- Session A: read
SELECT description, version FROM products WHERE product_id = 123;
-- suppose version = 5

-- Session B: update and commit
UPDATE products SET description = 'New by B', version = 6 WHERE product_id = 123 AND version = 5;

-- Session A: attempt update
UPDATE products SET description = 'New by A', version = 6 WHERE product_id = 123 AND version = 5;
-- If 0 rows affected -> conflict detected
Expected behavior
Session A's update should affect zero rows if Session B committed first; the app must then reload and resolve.
Common mistake
Not checking the rows-affected count allows silent overwrites. Always verify and handle zero-row updates.
Key Takeaway

Optimistic locking requires explicit conflict detection and a retry or merge strategy in your application.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we explore advanced concurrency strategies you’ll use to keep PostgreSQL systems fast and correct under load. We’ll compare pessimistic locking, where you acquire exclusive locks before modifying rows, with optimistic locking, where you detect conflicts at write time using a version or timestamp. You will see how PostgreSQL’s SELECT FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED and NOWAIT clauses let worker pools pick tasks without blocking, and we’ll study the invisible but critical danger of transaction ID wraparound and how VACUUM and autovacuum prevent it. Concrete examples include an accounts update using FOR UPDATE, an optimistic update that checks a version column, and a tasks queue demo showing two workers selecting different rows. I’ll also point out common mistakes — long-running transactions, excessive table-level locking, and unnecessary FOR UPDATE — and show which monitoring views to consult when things slow down. By the end you will know the trade-offs of each pattern, how to implement queue workers safely, and what to monitor so your database continues to operate reliably. How might you apply these patterns to the systems you manage, and which pitfall could cause the most trouble in your environment?

By the end of this chapter you will design application logic that uses both optimistic and pessimistic locking strategies, and you will know when each approach improves throughput or safety. You will implement queue processing that uses SELECT... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED or NOWAIT so worker pools avoid blocking and pick unique tasks. You will also understand transaction ID wraparound: why a 32-bit XID counter can roll over after roughly two billion transactions and why VACUUM and autovacuum must freeze old XIDs to keep visibility rules correct. Lastly, you will identify common concurrency pitfalls — long-running transactions, excessive locking, unnecessary FOR UPDATE, and deadlock-prone lock ordering — and apply monitoring techniques using pg_stat_activity, pg_locks and pg_stat_database to troubleshoot them. Each objective pairs a practical skill with the reason it matters, so you can both implement patterns safely and detect when they break under real load.

These objectives map to Bloom-style progression: you will learn core patterns, understand trade-offs between locking strategies, apply them in a queue-processing scenario, and move toward mastery by diagnosing and preventing XID wraparound. First, learn the mechanics: what SELECT FOR UPDATE does and how SKIP LOCKED affects row selection. Second, understand when optimistic locking is appropriate and how version column checks surface conflicts at write time. Third, apply SKIP LOCKED in a two-worker simulation to practice non-blocking task acquisition. Finally, master monitoring: routinely check xid_age in pg_stat_database and watch pg_locks for blocking chains. Each step pairs knowledge with practice so you can move from reading about techniques to reliably operating them in production. Consider which objective feels most urgent for your systems and start there — the monitoring objective is often highest priority for production teams.

Pessimistic locking is a pattern that assumes conflicts are likely and therefore holds locks before modifications occur. In PostgreSQL the canonical form is SELECT... FOR UPDATE, which acquires an exclusive lock on selected rows so other transactions cannot modify them until you commit or roll back. An everyday example is transferring funds between bank accounts: you might SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE account_id = 123 FOR UPDATE; then verify and write the new balance inside the same transaction. The benefit is correctness — you avoid lost updates — but the downside is blocking: other transactions that need the same rows will wait. A common misconception is that FOR UPDATE is always safer. In low-contention workloads it simply adds overhead and can cause unnecessary blocking because MVCC already isolates readers from writers. Use FOR UPDATE when you need strict serialization of a critical section, and keep transactions short to avoid holding locks for long periods. Key takeaway: pessimistic locking buys safety at the cost of throughput, so apply it only when conflict likelihood justifies the blocking behavior. How might you limit the window a lock is held in your application logic?

Optimistic locking assumes conflicts are rare and allows concurrent read and modify operations, detecting collisions only when a transaction writes. The typical implementation is to add a version column — an integer or a last_updated timestamp — to each row. When reading, the application records the current version. At update time it includes that original version in the WHERE clause and increments it. If another transaction updated the row in the meantime, the WHERE clause will match zero rows, signaling a conflict. For example, update products set stock = 9, version = 2 where product_id = 1 and version = 1; either the update affects one row and you succeed, or it affects zero rows and your application must retry or surface a conflict to the user. A common misconception is that optimistic locking eliminates the need to think about conflicts; it does not. You must design retry policies and user feedback paths, especially where updates are frequent. Optimistic locking maximizes concurrency in low-conflict workloads and shifts complexity into application logic for conflict handling. Optimistic Locking with Version Columns means detect conflicts at write-time using version checks; retry or resolve on zero-row updates.. In practical terms, detect conflicts at write time using versions or timestamps. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

When multiple workers consume tasks from a shared table, you want each worker to acquire a unique row without getting blocked by locks held by others. SELECT... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED is designed for exactly that. The pattern: start a transaction, select one pending job ordered by created_at using FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED LIMIT 1, then update the row to mark it processing and commit. SKIP LOCKED tells PostgreSQL to ignore rows that are already locked by another transaction instead of waiting. The practical result is that workers graze the queue and immediately claim available tasks, improving throughput and avoiding idle waiting. A concrete flow: Worker A begins and locks job 1; Worker B issues the same SELECT with SKIP LOCKED and PostgreSQL skips job 1 and returns job 2. Worker B can proceed without waiting for Worker A to commit. A common misconception is that SKIP LOCKED silently loses tasks; it does not lose rows, it only skips rows currently locked, so unprocessed tasks remain available. Use SKIP LOCKED for competing consumers when you prefer fast claim-over-wait semantics. The key question to reflect on: how will your application detect and re-enqueue jobs that fail after being claimed?

SELECT... FOR UPDATE NOWAIT and FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED are two related behaviors that differ in how they treat locked rows. NOWAIT immediately raises an error if a requested lock cannot be acquired; this is useful when you prefer to fail fast and handle the error rather than silently skip rows. SKIP LOCKED, by contrast, ignores locked rows and returns the next unlocked row, which is ideal for horizontally scaled worker pools. A concrete scenario clarifies the contrast: suppose a single consumer expects to process the next item in strict order; using NOWAIT ensures that if another process is handling that first item, your code gets an immediate error and can decide to retry or abort. In a multi-worker setup where order is unimportant, SKIP LOCKED lets workers continue processing other jobs without blocking. A common misconception is that NOWAIT is always unsafe; it’s not — it’s appropriate when ordering or strict ownership semantics matter and you want immediate feedback. Choose NOWAIT when you need explicit failure behavior and SKIP LOCKED when you favor availability and throughput. NOWAIT vs SKIP LOCKED means nowait fails fast on locked rows; skip locked skips locked rows and returns the next available one.. In practical terms, fail fast or skip locked rows — choose based on your failure semantics. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Let's walk through a concrete hands-on demonstration using the provided tasks table. Create the tasks table, insert a few pending tasks, then simulate two psql sessions. Worker 1 opens a transaction and runs SELECT... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED LIMIT 1; it locks one row but does not commit immediately. Worker 2 issues the same SELECT and, because SKIP LOCKED is in effect, it skips the locked row and returns the next pending row. Worker 2 updates its row and commits. Worker 1 then commits and updates its task. This sequence shows how SKIP LOCKED prevents workers from blocking on locked rows and enables high throughput. A common misconception is that this pattern loses tasks — it does not; locked rows remain visible to their locking transactions and will be committed or rollbacked, after which other workers may process remaining rows. After the demo, check the tasks table to verify that each worker processed a distinct row and review the S Q L outputs shown in the code panel. Hands-on: SKIP LOCKED with Two Workers means two simulated workers pick distinct tasks without blocking; skip locked yields immediate progress for each worker.. In practical terms, starter schema and session sequence to observe non-blocking picks. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

PostgreSQL assigns a 32-bit transaction ID (XID) to each transaction. Because it’s a fixed-size counter, after roughly two billion transactions the counter will wrap around. When wraparound occurs, PostgreSQL can no longer reliably decide whether an old row version is visible to a given transaction unless old XIDs are frozen. VACUUM — and the autovacuum daemon — periodically scan tables and mark very old XIDs as frozen, making those rows permanently visible for visibility checks. If autovacuum is not configured or long-running transactions prevent VACUUM from freezing rows, the database risks corruption or forced shutdown to avoid data integrity issues. Monitor pg_stat_database. datname and age(datfrozenxid) to see xid_age for your database. The common misconception is that VACUUM is optional; in practice autovacuum is essential to prevent wraparound. As a practical rule, ensure autovacuum runs regularly and investigate databases with high xid_age before they approach dangerous thresholds. Long-running transactions are one of the most damaging concurrency pitfalls. When a transaction remains open for hours or days it holds onto snapshot state and locks, preventing VACUUM from marking tuples as removable or freezing old XIDs. This leads to table bloat as dead row versions accumulate, and it can increase xid_age, bringing the database closer to wraparound risk. Excessive locking — especially coarse table-level locks — reduces parallelism and increases blocking and deadlocks. A common example is acquiring locks in inconsistent order across transactions; this pattern easily produces deadlocks under concurrent access. Another frequent mistake is blanket use of FOR UPDATE on many rows when only a simple SELECT would suffice; this adds unnecessary lock contention. To mitigate these issues, keep transactions short, avoid manual long transactions in application code, use row-level locking when possible, and acquire locks in a consistent order. Regularly examine pg_stat_activity for idle-in-transaction sessions and pg_locks for blocking chains so you can quickly identify and resolve these problems. When concurrency issues appear you must be able to inspect what the server is doing. pg_stat_activity shows active sessions, their state, and query text so you can spot long-running or idle-in-transaction sessions. pg_locks reveals which locks are held and which processes are waiting; it helps you trace blocking chains. pg_stat_statements identifies heavy or frequently contended queries for optimization. A concrete troubleshooting workflow: query pg_stat_activity to find sessions with long durations, join to pg_locks to see which sessions are waiting for locks and which sessions hold those locks, and use pg_stat_statements to find the offending query text and plan characteristics. A common misconception is that killing a waiting session always fixes the problem; sometimes the blocker is the session holding a lock, not the waiter. This screen collects practical design rules that reduce concurrency problems. First, always acquire locks in a consistent global order to avoid deadlocks — pick a deterministic ordering of resources and stick to it across transactions. Second, keep transactions short: do not perform long-running external calls while holding database locks or doing important updates. Third, prefer row-level locks instead of table-level locks when you need to serialize updates. Fourth, instrument and monitor: alert on idle-in-transaction sessions and rising xid_age. Fifth, for worker queues use SKIP LOCKED and implement a robust failure/retry policy so claimed tasks are retried if a worker crashes. A frequent misconception is that more aggressive locking configurations will always increase safety; in fact, coarse locks often reduce throughput and lead to cascading waits. The end takeaway is to make small, incremental changes: tune autovacuum, standardize lock order, shorten transactions, and add visibility through monitoring queries. This lab asks you to implement optimistic locking for a products table using a version column and to exercise a conflict. Steps: add version INT to products, read the current description and version in one session, then in a second session update the same row and commit. In the first session attempt an UPDATE that includes the original version in the WHERE clause and increments the version. If the UPDATE affects zero rows you have detected a conflict and should retry or present the user with the latest data. The purpose is to observe the optimistic pattern: concurrent reads proceed, and only conflicting writes force application-level conflict resolution. A common mistake is to forget to check the rows-affected count after the UPDATE; without that check the application will assume success and silently lose changes. Here are the essential concepts to retain. First, optimistic locking detects conflicts at write time using a version or timestamp; it maximizes concurrency but requires application-level conflict resolution. Second, pessimistic locking with SELECT FOR UPDATE acquires locks ahead of modification to ensure serializable updates; it is simple and safe but can reduce throughput if used indiscriminately. Third, SELECT... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED enables high-throughput worker pools by skipping locked rows, while NOWAIT fails fast when locks can’t be acquired. Also remember the administration side: monitor xid_age with pg_stat_database and keep autovacuum healthy to prevent XID wraparound.
